domain:
    # Single problem size N used for both i and j
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Matrix A: logically A[i, j], used both as A[i, j] and A[j, i]
    # Store A in row-major order (j is the fastest-varying index) to make
    #   the A[i, j] access in phase 1 contiguous in memory.
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Vectors (1D over i)
    # x1 and x2 are updated in-place (accumulation), y1 and y2 are read-only
    x1[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
    x2[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
    y1[i]: in    DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i   # corresponds to y_1 in the code
    y2[i]: in    DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i   # corresponds to y_2 in the code

parameters:
    N   : size_t          # common vector/matrix dimension (N = n in the code)
    T_I : size_t          # tile size for i (rows), tunable (e.g., 32 or 64)
    T_J : size_t          # tile size for j (columns), tunable (e.g., 64)
    V_J : size_t          # SIMD vector width used on j (<= hardware SIMD width)

computation:
    # Phase 1 in the C++ code:
    #   for i in 0..N-1:
    #     for j in 0..N-1:
    #       x1[i] += A[i][j] * y_1[j];
    #
    # We express it as a per-i reduction to make the accumulation into x1[i]
    # explicit and to enable using a register accumulator per i.
    phase1:
        for i in [0, N):
            x1[i] = x1[i] + sum(j in [0, N), A[i, j] * y1[j])

    # Phase 2 in the C++ code:
    #   for i in 0..N-1:
    #     for j in 0..N-1:
    #       x2[i] += A[j][i] * y_2[j];
    #
    # This is a matrix–vector product with the transpose: x2 = x2 + A^T * y2.
    phase2:
        for i in [0, N):
            x2[i] = x2[i] + sum(j in [0, N), A[j, i] * y2[j])

dependencies:
    # Phase 1 and Phase 2 operate on disjoint outputs (x1 vs x2) and do not
    # depend on each other’s results, but the original program executes them
    # in sequence. We preserve that ordering here.
    for i in [0, N):
        phase1(i) -> phase2(i)

optimization:
    #---------------------------------------------
    # 1. Tiling / blocking to improve cache usage
    #---------------------------------------------
    # We tile both i and j:
    #   - i is the reduction output index for both phases (x1[i], x2[i]).
    #   - j is the reduction index.
    # Tiling i improves locality in the x1/x2 vectors for very large N.
    # Tiling j improves locality in y1/y2 and reduces the working-set size
    #   of the A rows/columns seen in the innermost loops.
    block(i, I, T_I)   # I indexes tiles of rows, each of height T_I
    block(j, J, T_J)   # J indexes tiles of columns, each of width T_J

    # After blocking, a generic loop nest has the shape:
    #   for I:
    #     for J:
    #       for i in tile I:
    #         for j in tile J:
    #           ...
    #
    # We hoist I and J to the outermost levels so that we iterate over tiles first.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    #---------------------------------------------
    # 2. Loop structure within tiles and SIMD
    #---------------------------------------------
    # Inside each (I, J) tile, we keep j as the innermost loop. With the chosen
    # row‑major layout (A[i, j] -> i * N + j), this makes accesses to A[i, j]
    # in phase 1 contiguous in memory and enables efficient vectorization.
    #
    # The access A[j, i] in phase 2 is necessarily strided in one dimension for
    # any single-layout matrix (since it uses the transpose), but tiling still
    # improves temporal locality: for a fixed tile (I, J), the rows/columns
    # touched by phase 2 stay resident in cache while the tile is processed.

    # Vectorize the innermost j-loop inside each (I, J) tile in both phases:
    #   - The compiler can map this to SIMD loads of A[i, j] and y1[j] in phase 1,
    #     and SIMD loads of A[j, i] and y2[j] in phase 2.
    vectorize(j, V_J)

    # Optionally unroll the j loop further to reduce loop overhead and to give the
    # compiler more freedom to schedule FMA instructions.
    unroll(j, V_J)

    #---------------------------------------------
    # 3. Register accumulators for reductions
    #---------------------------------------------
    # The "sum(...)" in the computation section already expresses that j is a
    # reduction dimension. Implementations should:
    #   - For each (I, i) tile row, keep a scalar accumulator in a register:
    #         acc1 = x1[i];  acc2 = x2[i];
    #     and only write back x1[i], x2[i] once per tile / per i.
    #   - This replaces repeated loads/stores of x1[i] / x2[i] inside the j-loop
    #     with register updates, reducing memory traffic and enabling FMA.

    #---------------------------------------------
    # 4. Parallelization
    #---------------------------------------------
    # For both phases, different values of i are independent:
    #   - x1[i] is only updated in phase 1(i, *),
    #   - x2[i] is only updated in phase 2(i, *),
    # and there are no cross-i dependencies.
    #
    # Therefore we parallelize across i-tiles (I). Each thread (or core) can
    # process one or more I-tiles, handling all j-tiles (J) for those rows.
    # This maps well onto a 32-core / 64-thread machine.
    parallelize(I)

    # NOTE: We deliberately do NOT parallelize across j or J without additional
    # temporary buffers, because x1[i] and x2[i] are reductions over j. Splitting
    # j across threads would require per-thread partial sums and an explicit
    # reduction step. Such a scheme is possible but would need extra temporary
    # storage; here we keep memory usage minimal and always within 50% of the
    # original footprint by only parallelizing i.

```text
domain:
    # Problem size (square matrix, all vectors of length N)
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row / vector index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index

data:
    # Store A in row‑major order to make A[i, j] contiguous in j.
    # This improves cache behavior for the first MV and, combined with tiling,
    # gives good locality for the second MV as well.
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE
        = (i, j) -> i * N + j           # row-major: row i is contiguous

    # Vectors are stored contiguously
    x1[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i   # x1 is updated in kernel
    x2[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i   # x2 is updated in kernel
    y1[j]: in    DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j   # y_1 in code
    y2[j]: in    DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j   # y_2 in code

parameters:
    N:  int                  # problem size
    TI: int                  # tile size in i (rows), tuning parameter
    TJ: int                  # tile size in j (cols), tuning parameter
    VW: int                  # SIMD width for j-vectorization (e.g., 4 or 8)

computation:
    # First part of MVT:
    #   for i = 0..N-1:
    #     x1[i] += sum_{j=0..N-1} A[i, j] * y1[j]
    #
    # Use an explicit accumulator to avoid repeated loads/stores of x1[i].
    mv1:
        for i in seq(0, N):
            acc1 = x1[i]
            for j in [0, N):
                acc1 = acc1 + A[i, j] * y1[j]
            x1[i] = acc1

    # Second part of MVT:
    #   for i = 0..N-1:
    #     x2[i] += sum_{j=0..N-1} A[j, i] * y2[j]
    #
    # This keeps the mathematical definition from the original code (x2 is the
    # product with A^T). The use of an accumulator again minimizes memory
    # traffic on x2.
    mv2:
        for i in seq(0, N):
            acc2 = x2[i]
            for j in [0, N):
                acc2 = acc2 + A[j, i] * y2[j]
            x2[i] = acc2

dependencies:
    # Within each mv1 / mv2 iteration, acc1/acc2 is a scalar reduction over j.
    # Different i-iterations are independent:
    #   - mv1(i) only writes x1[i]
    #   - mv2(i) only writes x2[i]
    #
    # This allows safe parallelization over i.
    for i in [0, N):
        mv1(i) -> mv1(i)   # intra-iteration j-order is a reduction; no cross-i deps
        mv2(i) -> mv2(i)

optimization:
    #----------------------------
    # Global data-layout choices
    #----------------------------
    # A is chosen row-major: (i, j) -> i * N + j. This:
    #   - Makes mv1’s inner j-loop access A[i, j] with unit stride.
    #   - Allows mv2 to be tiled in (j, i) and still get good spatial locality
    #     for A across tiles, even though it needs A[j, i].
    #
    # Vectors are already contiguous; no further layout changes are needed.

    #----------------------------
    # Optimizations for mv1
    #   x1[i] += sum_j A[i, j] * y1[j]
    #----------------------------

    # 1) Tile both i and j to improve cache reuse and expose parallelism.
    #    I1: tile index over i, inner i remains the in-tile row index.
    #    J1: tile index over j, inner j remains the in-tile column index.
    block(mv1.i, I1, TI)
    block(mv1.j, J1, TJ)

    # 2) Order tiles as:
    #       for I1 (outer, parallel)
    #         for J1
    #           for i in tile I1
    #             for j in tile J1
    #    This keeps each thread working on a contiguous chunk of rows (good
    #    for x1) and walks A row-wise inside each tile.
    hoist(mv1.I1)
    hoist(mv1.J1)

    # 3) Parallelize across row tiles: each tile I1 owns a disjoint set of
    #    rows, so it writes a disjoint segment of x1 and only reads A, y1.
    parallelize(mv1.I1)

    # 4) Vectorize the innermost j-loop:
    #    Inside a tile, A[i, j] and y1[j] are contiguous in j. This allows
    #    efficient SIMD loads and FMAs along j.
    vectorize(mv1.j, VW)

    #----------------------------
    # Optimizations for mv2
    #   x2[i] += sum_j A[j, i] * y2[j]
    #----------------------------

    # 1) Tile the (i, j) space similarly. For mv2 we still conceptually
    #    compute per-row reductions in i, but tiling j improves cache reuse
    #    on A and y2.
    block(mv2.i, I2, TI)
    block(mv2.j, J2, TJ)

    # 2) Keep I2 outermost so each worker processes whole row blocks and
    #    writes disjoint ranges of x2. J2 is the next outer loop.
    hoist(mv2.I2)
    hoist(mv2.J2)

    # 3) Parallelize over row tiles also here; tiles in I2 do not share x2
    #    elements, and all read-only data (A, y2) can be shared safely.
    parallelize(mv2.I2)

    # 4) Vectorize the inner j-loop over tiles:
    #    Even though mv2 accesses A[j, i], tiling ensures that within a J2-tile
    #    the stride in the memory layout is small and regular. This lets the
    #    compiler generate SIMD loads for A[j, i] and y2[j], and accumulate
    #    into the scalar acc2.
    vectorize(mv2.j, VW)

    #---------------------------------------------------------
    # Notes on arithmetic and memory-traffic optimizations
    #---------------------------------------------------------
    # - Using acc1 and acc2 avoids reloading and storing x1[i] / x2[i] on every
    #   inner iteration: we load once per i, accumulate in a register, and
    #   store once at the end.
    # - Tiling with (TI, TJ) reduces working-set size per tile:
    #     * A tile touches TI rows and TJ columns of A: TI * TJ elements.
    #     * The corresponding slices of y1 or y2 are TJ elements.
    #     * The portion of x1/x2 touched is TI elements.
    #   Properly chosen TI, TJ (e.g., so that A-tile + vector slices fit in
    #   L1/L2) significantly reduces cache misses.
    # - Parallelization is restricted to I1 / I2 (row tiles), which guarantees
    #   that no two threads update the same x1[i] or x2[i], so no extra
    #   synchronization is required.
    # - No extra full-size copies of A are introduced; all temporaries are
    #   scalar accumulators or data already in registers / caches. Additional
    #   memory overhead is negligible compared to the original footprint and
    #   stays far below the allowed +50%.
```

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)        # primary 1D index (size N)
    j: dim in [0, N)        # second 1D index (size N)

data:
    # All vectors are stored as unit-stride 1D arrays.
    x1[i]: inout num_t = (i) -> i
    x2[i]: inout num_t = (i) -> i
    y1[j]: in    num_t = (j) -> j
    y2[j]: in    num_t = (j) -> j

    # Matrix A is stored row-major in (i,j):
    #   A[i,j] is at address base_A + (i * N + j)
    A[i, j]: in num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters (chosen based on cache & SIMD width of the target CPU):
    Ti: positive int    # tile size for i-dimension (e.g., 64..256)
    Tj: positive int    # tile size for j-dimension (e.g., 64..256)
    Vi: positive int    # SIMD width for i-dimension vectorization (for S2 inner loop)
    Vj: positive int    # SIMD width for j-dimension vectorization (for S1 inner loop)

computation:
    # S1: x1 <- x1 + A * y1
    #     for (i = 0..N-1) for (j = 0..N-1) x1[i] += A[i,j] * y1[j];
    S1:
        for i in [0, N):
            acc1 = x1[i]                         # accumulate x1[i] in a register
            for j in [0, N):
                acc1 = acc1 + A[i, j] * y1[j]
            x1[i] = acc1                         # single write-back to memory

    # S2: x2 <- x2 + A^T * y2
    # Original code:
    #   for (i) for (j) x2[i] += A[j,i] * y2[j];
    # We interchange (i,j) to improve locality for A[j,i] (row-major in j):
    S2:
        for j in [0, N):
            tmp2 = y2[j]                         # reuse y2[j] within inner loop
            for i in [0, N):
                x2[i] = x2[i] + A[j, i] * tmp2   # A[j,i] accessed with unit stride over i

dependencies:
    # S1 and S2 are independent:
    # - both read A, y1, y2
    # - S1 writes only x1; S2 writes only x2
    # so they can be reordered or executed concurrently if desired.
    # No explicit cross-statement dependencies are required.

optimization:
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Loop tiling (blocking) to improve cache reuse of A and y[*]
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # block_in(L, dim, tile_dim, tile_size) means:
    #   - In statement L, replace 'dim' with two nested dimensions:
    #       tile_dim in seq([0, ceil(|dim| / tile_size)))
    #       dim      in seq(tile_dim * tile_size,
    #                       min((tile_dim + 1) * tile_size, |dim|))
    #   - All occurrences of 'dim' in L are understood as 'inner dim'
    #     inside the tile.
    #
    # Apply symmetric tiling in both i and j for both S1 and S2.
    block_in(S1, i, I, Ti)
    block_in(S1, j, J, Tj)
    block_in(S2, i, I, Ti)
    block_in(S2, j, J, Tj)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Loop order / hoisting for better locality
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # For S1 (x1 <- x1 + A * y1):
    #   - We want inner-most loop over j to exploit row-major A[i,j].
    #   - A good tiled order is: for I, for i in tile, for J, for j in tile.
    # hoist_in(L, dim) means move 'dim' as far out as legality allows in L.
    hoist_in(S1, I)         # iterate row tiles outermost
    hoist_in(S1, J)         # then column tiles
    # (Within each (I,J) tile, the order is i then j, so j remains innermost.)

    # For S2 (x2 <- x2 + A^T * y2):
    #   - We already interchanged loops so that outer loop is j and inner is i.
    #   - For cache locality of A[j,i], we prefer to traverse tiles in J-major order.
    #   - A good tiled order is: for J, for j in tile, for I, for i in tile.
    hoist_in(S2, J)         # iterate column tiles outermost
    hoist_in(S2, I)         # then row tiles

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization and unrolling
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # vectorize(dim, factor) means:
    #   - generate SIMD code over 'dim' with lane width 'factor'
    #   - handle remainder iterations with a scalar cleanup loop.
    # unroll(dim, factor) means:
    #   - unroll the loop over 'dim' by 'factor' for better ILP/FMA utilization.
    #
    # S1: inner j-loop is a natural candidate for SIMD over contiguous A[i,j] and y1[j].
    vectorize(j, Vj)
    unroll(j, 4)

    # S2: inner i-loop can be SIMD-ized over x2[i] and A[j,i], which are unit-stride in i.
    vectorize(i, Vi)
    unroll(i, 4)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelization
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # parallelize_in(L, dim) means:
    #   - loop(s) over 'dim' in statement L are executed in parallel,
    #     assuming iterations over 'dim' have no cross-dependencies.
    #
    # S1: iterations over i are independent reductions into distinct x1[i].
    parallelize_in(S1, I)   # distribute row tiles of S1 across cores

    # S2: for fixed j, iterations over i update distinct x2[i] and are independent.
    #      We parallelize over i (or its tiled version I) inside each j-iteration.
    parallelize_in(S2, I)

    # Note: No additional large temporary buffers are introduced.
    # - Only scalar temporaries (acc1, tmp2) are used.
    # - Tiling and parallelization operate directly on A, x1, x2, y1, y2.
    # - Memory footprint stays within the original arrays plus negligible scalar state
    #   (< 50% overhead as required).
```

Optimized model description:

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)           # logical row / vector index
    j: dim in [0, N)           # logical column / vector index

data:
    # Matrix A: A[i,j] in row-major layout
    #   - i = row index
    #   - j = column index
    #   - matches: DEFINE_PROTO_STRUCT(a_layout, j_vec ^ i_vec)
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Vectors x1, x2: 1D over i (both read and written)
    x1[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i -> i
    x2[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i -> i

    # Vectors y1, y2: 1D over j (read‑only in the kernel)
    # In the original code, these are stored over dimension 'i' and then
    # viewed as 'j' via rename<'i','j'>; semantically this is y[ j ] here.
    y1[j]: in DATA_TYPE = j -> j
    y2[j]: in DATA_TYPE = j -> j

parameters:
    N: int                         # problem size (N x N matrix, N-length vectors)

    # Tunable constants for cache/blocking and SIMD; chosen per target machine.
    BI1: int                       # tile size for i in part1 (x1 update)
    BJ1: int                       # tile size for j in part1
    BI2: int                       # tile size for i in part2 (x2 update)
    BJ2: int                       # tile size for j in part2
    V1:  int                       # unroll / vector width for j in part1
    V2:  int                       # unroll / vector width for i in part2

computation:
    part1:
        # First loop nest in kernel_mvt:
        #   for i in [0,N):
        #     for j in [0,N):
        #       x1[i] += A[i,j] * y1[j];
        #
        # Expressed with an explicit reduction so the implementation can
        # keep a per‑i accumulator in a register (avoids repeated loads/stores
        # of x1[i] inside the inner loop):
        for i in seq(0, N):
            x1[i] = x1[i] + sum(j in [0, N), A[i, j] * y1[j])

    part2:
        # Second loop nest in kernel_mvt:
        #   for i in [0,N):
        #     for j in [0,N):
        #       x2[i] += A[j,i] * y2[j];
        #
        # This sums, for each i, over all rows j of A, using column i:
        for i in seq(0, N):
            x2[i] = x2[i] + sum(j in [0, N), A[j, i] * y2[j])

    # Note: part1 and part2 touch disjoint output vectors (x1 vs x2), and both
    # use A, y1, y2 read‑only, so they are independent and may execute in
    # any order or in parallel without changing the mathematical result.

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # General note on reduction implementation
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The use of sum(...) in both parts indicates an implementation that:
    #   - Loads x1[i] or x2[i] once before the inner loop,
    #   - Accumulates into a local scalar register,
    #   - Stores the final value back after the inner loop.
    # This removes repeated memory traffic for x1[i]/x2[i] present in the
    # straightforward "x[i] = x[i] + ..." formulation.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Coarse‑grain task parallelism
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # New directive:
    #   task_parallelize(P, Q):
    #       run labeled computations P and Q as independent tasks in
    #       separate threads, with no ordering constraints between them.
    #
    # Here, part1 and part2 are independent (x1 vs x2), so we can overlap
    # the two matrix‑vector products on different cores:
    task_parallelize(part1, part2)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Optimizations for part1 (x1[i] += sum_j A[i,j] * y1[j])
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Memory behavior:
    #   - A[i, j] is row‑major: j is the contiguous (fast‑varying) index.
    #   - The original code already iterates with i outer, j inner, which is
    #     cache‑friendly for A and sequential for y1.
    #
    # We make this more explicit and add blocking, SIMD, and parallelism.

    # 1. Tile the (i, j) iteration space so tiles fit better into caches.
    #    This keeps portions of A and y1 hot while updating a band of x1.
    block(i, I1, BI1)              # I1 indexes tiles of rows (bands of i)
    block(j, J1, BJ1)              # J1 indexes tiles of columns (subranges of j)

    # 2. Make the row‑tile loop outermost so each tile of rows is processed
    #    as a unit, improving spatial locality in A and x1.
    hoist(I1)

    # 3. Parallelize across independent row tiles. Each tile I1 corresponds
    #    to a disjoint subset of x1[i], so no synchronization is required.
    parallelize(I1)

    # 4. Improve single‑core performance inside each tile:
    #    - Unroll and SIMD‑vectorize the inner J1 loop, which walks the
    #      contiguous j‑dimension.
    unroll(J1, V1)
    vectorize(J1, V1)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Optimizations for part2 (x2[i] += sum_j A[j,i] * y2[j])
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # In the original code, this is implemented as:
    #   for i: for j: x2[i] += A[j,i] * y2[j];
    # which, with A row‑major in (i,j), accesses A with a stride of N
    # (column‑major pattern) and is cache‑unfriendly.
    #
    # We first change the traversal order to walk rows of A contiguously,
    # then tile and parallelize carefully to avoid races on x2.

    # 1. Loop interchange inside part2:
    #    Transform the conceptual nest to:
    #        for j in [0,N):        # outer
    #            for i in [0,N):    # inner
    #                x2[i] += A[j,i] * y2[j];
    #
    #    Now, for each fixed j, A[j, i] is accessed with i as the
    #    contiguous dimension (row j of A), giving good spatial locality
    #    and reusing y2[j] across all i.
    interchange(i, j)              # applied to the part2 loops only

    # 2. Tile the transformed (j, i) space.
    #    - J2 tiles rows of A (blocks of j),
    #    - I2 tiles columns (bands of i / segments of x2).
    block(j, J2, BJ2)
    block(i, I2, BI2)

    # 3. Make J2 (row tiles) outermost to stream over blocks of rows and
    #    reuse y2[j] and A[j,*] within each tile.
    hoist(J2)

    # 4. Parallelization strategy for part2:
    #    We split the i‑dimension into disjoint bands I2 and assign each
    #    band to a different thread. Each thread:
    #      - iterates over all j (and J2 tiles of j),
    #      - updates only its own slice x2[i in I2].
    #    This avoids any write conflicts on x2 without extra buffers and
    #    keeps extra memory usage negligible (only thread‑local scalars).
    parallelize(I2)

    # 5. Within each (J2, I2) tile, use SIMD along I2. For fixed j, A[j,i]
    #    is contiguous in i, so we can unroll and vectorize over I2 to
    #    generate efficient vector loads and fused mul‑add instructions.
    unroll(I2, V2)
    vectorize(I2, V2)
```

```text
domain:
    # N is the common problem size from defines.hpp
    i: dim in [0, N)  # row-like index
    j: dim in [0, N)  # column-like index

data:
    # Dense N×N matrix A, row-major in (i, j):
    #   A[i, j] is stored at offset i * N + j.
    A[i, j]: in num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Vectors; all are length-N and stored contiguously.
    # We associate x1, x2 with i, and y_1, y_2 with j to match the kernels.
    x1[i]: inout num_t = i      # corresponds to C++ x1
    x2[i]: inout num_t = i      # corresponds to C++ x2
    y_1[j]: in num_t = j        # corresponds to C++ y_1 (viewed as y_1_j)
    y_2[j]: in num_t = j        # corresponds to C++ y_2 (viewed as y_2_j)

parameters:
    N: int                      # problem size
    # Tuning constants; chosen to respect cache sizes and vector width.
    TJ: int                     # tile size for inner j-dimension in A * y_1
    TI2: int                    # tile size for i-dimension in A^T * y_2
    VEC_J: int                  # SIMD width for j (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 4 for double)
    VEC_I: int                  # SIMD width for i in the blocked transpose kernel
    P: int                      # number of parallel workers (<= number of cores)

computation:
    # First kernel: x1 += A * y_1
    # Equivalent to the C++:
    #   for (i) for (j) x1[i] += A[i][j] * y_1[j];
    Lx1: for i in [0, N):
            # Reduction over j; x1[i] is updated once per i.
            x1[i] = x1[i] + sum(j in [0, N): A[i, j] * y_1[j])

    # Second kernel: x2 += A^T * y_2
    # Equivalent to the C++:
    #   for (i) for (j) x2[i] += A[j][i] * y_2[j];
    Lx2: for i in [0, N):
            x2[i] = x2[i] + sum(j in [0, N): A[j, i] * y_2[j])

dependencies:
    # Within Lx1 and Lx2:
    # - Each i-iteration only updates x1[i] or x2[i], respectively.
    # - The reductions over j are purely local to that i.
    # So iterations over different i are independent.
    for i in [0, N):
        Lx1(i) -> Lx1(i)
        Lx2(i) -> Lx2(i)

    # x1 and x2 are disjoint outputs; A, y_1, and y_2 are read-only in the kernels.
    # Therefore Lx1 and Lx2 may be executed in any order or even concurrently.
    no dependency between Lx1 and Lx2

optimization:
    # We extend the optimization language with loop- and kernel-local directives:
    #
    #   block_in(L, D, T, B):
    #       Block dimension D in loop nest L into an outer tile index T and an inner
    #       index D (D = T * B + D_inner) with tile size B.
    #
    #   parallelize_in(L, D):
    #       Parallelize loop nest L across dimension D (typically the outermost loop
    #       in that nest), assigning disjoint chunks of D to different threads.
    #
    #   vectorize_in(L, D, W):
    #       Vectorize the innermost loop over dimension D in L using SIMD width W.
    #       W should divide the tile size used for D so that each SIMD iteration
    #       operates on a full vector.
    #
    #   accum_in_registers(L, D):
    #       For each iteration over index D in L, keep the corresponding x-element
    #       (x1[D] or x2[D]) in a scalar accumulator register while iterating the
    #       reduction dimension, and write it back only once per D.
    #
    #   blocked_transpose_mvt(L, OUT_D, SUM_D, B):
    #       Specialize a kernel of the form
    #           x[OUT_D] += sum(SUM_D, A[SUM_D, OUT_D] * y[SUM_D])
    #       into a blocked algorithm over OUT_D with block size B:
    #         - Split OUT_D into tiles of size B: OUT_D = T * B + d (d in [0, B)).
    #         - For each tile T, allocate a small temporary array acc[d] (size B).
    #         - Initialize acc[d] from x[OUT_D] for d in the tile.
    #         - Sweep SUM_D from 0..N-1; in the inner loop update acc[d] using
    #           A[SUM_D, OUT_D] and y[SUM_D]. The inner-most loop is over d,
    #           so A[SUM_D, OUT_D] is accessed contiguously in memory w.r.t. OUT_D.
    #         - After the SUM_D loop, write acc[d] back to x[OUT_D] for the tile.
    #       This preserves the mathematical result but:
    #         * turns the strided A[j, i] access of Lx2 into mostly contiguous access
    #           along OUT_D (i),
    #         * reduces repeated loads/stores of x[OUT_D] to one load and one store
    #           per OUT_D index,
    #         * uses extra memory proportional to B (and at most P * B if each thread
    #           has a private buffer), which stays well below 50% of the original
    #           footprint provided B << N.

    # --- First kernel: x1 += A * y_1 ---

    # Keep x1[i] in a scalar accumulator while summing over j, to avoid repeated
    # loads and stores to x1[i] in the inner loop.
    accum_in_registers(Lx1, i)

    # Tile the j-dimension to align with cache lines and SIMD vectors.
    # Within each i, the inner loops operate on contiguous subranges A[i, j:j+TJ)
    # and y_1[j:j+TJ).
    block_in(Lx1, j, J1, TJ)

    # Vectorize the innermost j-loop inside each tile using VEC_J-wide SIMD.
    vectorize_in(Lx1, j, VEC_J)

    # Parallelize across rows i: different i-iterations touch disjoint x1[i] and
    # sum over the same read-only A and y_1. This maps naturally to OpenMP/TBB
    # parallel_for over i or over tiles of i.
    parallelize_in(Lx1, i)

    # --- Second kernel: x2 += A^T * y_2 ---

    # Use a blocked algorithm for the transpose matrix–vector product, so that
    # A[j, i] is accessed in contiguous chunks along i and x2 is updated from
    # small per-tile accumulators.
    blocked_transpose_mvt(Lx2, i, j, TI2)

    # Vectorize the inner i-loop inside each tile and SUM_D iteration using VEC_I.
    # This lets the compiler generate wide loads/stores for x2-accumulators and
    # the corresponding row segments of A.
    vectorize_in(Lx2, i, VEC_I)

    # Parallelize across tiles of i (OUT_D): different tiles update disjoint
    # segments of x2 and only read A and y_2, so they can be safely assigned
    # to different threads.
    parallelize_in(Lx2, i)
```
